Ball-tree builders¶

This page documents the geometry-aware ball-tree builders introduced in src/trees together with the helper utilities they share. It collects the intuition behind each construction algorithm, summarises the most relevant complexity bounds, and explains how the test-suite exercises the implementation.

All builders operate on dense numpy.ndarray inputs, reuse the common Node data model, and rely on the same minimum enclosing ball (MEB) primitives. Configuration dictionaries are loaded from configs and can be overridden per call.

Helper utilities¶

Minimum enclosing ball (utils.meb)¶

  • meb() is a thin dispatcher that selects either the fast Ritter approximation or Welzl’s exact algorithm based on config["meb"]. Dispatching itself is \(O(1)\) and every builder calls it exactly once per node.

  • ritter() implements the classic two-pass heuristic [Omohundro1989]. It scans the point set a constant number of times and therefore runs in \(O(m d)\) time for \(m\) points of dimension \(d\). Builders use it for leaf nodes (when meb="ritter"), for heuristic balance evaluation in gal.trees.pca_ballstar, and during pre-clustering in gal.trees.bottom_up.

  • welzl() follows Welzl’s recursive incremental algorithm [Welzl1991] with an expected \(O(m d)\) running time. It is chosen whenever config["meb"] == "welzl" and guarantees exact leaf balls. Internally it depends on _ball_from_support(), which solves the support-system via dense linear algebra; those solves are bounded by \(O(d^3)\) but the support set never exceeds \(d+1\) points.

Geometry helpers (utils.geometry)¶

  • enclose_two_balls() and enclose_many_balls() are used whenever a parent node is created. The two-ball enclosure is \(O(d)\), while the accumulation over \(k\) children is \(O(k d)\). All builders therefore inherit the \(O(d)\) per-node cost for updating parent radii.

  • centroid() provides the mean vector in gal.trees.two_pivot; the computation is \(O(m d)\) for the active index view.

  • project() realises projection onto a unit vector for gal.trees.pca_ballstar, costing \(O(m d)\).

  • dist2() is used indirectly inside the MEB routines and has constant \(O(d)\) cost.

Partition helpers (utils.partitions)¶

  • nth_element_inplace() and axis_median_split() wrap numpy.argpartition() to supply \(O(m)\) median splits without allocating intermediate arrays. gal.trees.axis_median, gal.trees.two_pivot (for degeneracy handling), and gal.trees.bottom_up all reuse them.

  • direction_quantile_splits() partitions projections into quantile bins in \(O(m)\) time. It is central to the k-ary general cases in gal.trees.pca_ballstar and gal.trees.axis_median (when max_children > 2).

Ball-tree construction methods¶

Axis-aligned median splits¶

Module: gal.trees.axis_median.

Intuition (after [Omohundro1989]): split along the coordinate with the largest spread so that sibling subtrees are balanced by count. The builder evaluates \(\mathrm{ptp}\) to find the widest axis, partitions indices using axis_median_split(), and wraps each child in an MEB.

Helper interplay:

  • Axis selection uses numpy’s ptp on the view created by the recursion.

  • Leaves call meb() with the configured backend.

  • Internal nodes aggregate child balls with enclose_many_balls().

Complexity: the recursion performs one \(O(m)\) partition per level, so the expected running time is \(O(n \log n \cdot d)\) for balanced inputs with \(n\) points of dimension \(d\).

Two-pivot / max-diameter splits¶

Module: gal.trees.two_pivot.

Intuition (after [Moore2000]): choose a pair of far-apart pivots and assign points to the nearer ball so that siblings are tight. Degenerate cases fall back to axis or directional medians to keep both sides non-empty.

Helper interplay:

  • centroid() establishes the reference point for picking the farthest pivot.

  • Farthest-point seeding for multi-way splits reuses vectorised distance computations and, when needed, axis_median_split() as a safety net.

  • As in all other builders, child balls are combined via enclose_many_balls().

Complexity: farthest-point seeding scans the current subset a constant number of times (\(O(m d)\)), the Voronoi assignment is \(O(m k d)\) for \(k\) children, and the tree as a whole remains \(O(n \log n \cdot d)\) for the binary default.

PCA / Ball* splits¶

Module: gal.trees.pca_ballstar.

Intuition (after [Dolatshah2015]): align the split with the dominant principal component and - optionally - refine the threshold to minimise the sum of child radii (Ball* criterion).

Helper interplay:

  • power PCA uses iterative multiplication by the covariance matrix with RNG seeding; the fallback svd option calls numpy.linalg.svd().

  • Projections reuse project(), and quantile slicing uses direction_quantile_splits().

  • Balance refinement invokes ritter() on candidate halves to evaluate the radius surrogate quickly.

Complexity: computing the first component via power iteration is \(O(p \cdot m d)\) for pca_iters = p. The median split and MEB calls contribute \(O(m d)\). Overall the builder is near \(O(n \log n \cdot d)\) while offering tighter sibling balls.

Bottom-up agglomeration¶

Module: gal.trees.bottom_up.

Intuition (after [Omohundro1989]): start from very small clusters and merge the most compatible pair at each step so that node radii stay compact. An optional pre-clustering stage reduces the number of leaf nodes for large inputs.

Helper interplay:

  • precluster_leaf_size controls a preliminary top-down pass that reuses axis_median_split() and the MEB helpers.

  • During agglomeration every merge computes enclose_many_balls() to evaluate cost proxies such as radius or delta-radius.

Complexity: with singleton pre-clusters the naive pairwise search is \(O(n^2 d)\) merges; picking the optimal partner also incurs \(O(n^2)\) comparisons. The implementation is intentionally simple, with a TODO note for NN-chain acceleration.

Middle-out anchors hierarchy¶

Module: gal.trees.middle_out.

Intuition (after [Moore2000]): seed the space with far-apart anchors, grow a balanced core by merging the most compatible anchor groups, and recursively refine oversized leaves. This “middle-out” strategy combines tight balls with well-balanced depth.

Helper interplay:

  • Farthest-point seeding mirrors the logic in gal.trees.two_pivot, repeatedly applying vectorised distance scans.

  • Anchor assignments loop through numpy distance computations and reuse the MEB dispatcher for every anchor cluster.

  • Agglomeration mirrors gal.trees.bottom_up, relying on enclose_many_balls() to score candidate groups.

Complexity: building \(k\) anchors from \(m\) points costs \(O(k m d)\) per assignment round. The hierarchical merging behaves like \(O(k^2 d)\) for the number of anchor nodes. Recursive leaf refinement only triggers when a leaf exceeds leaf_size.

Disjoint Greedy¶

Module: gal.trees.disjoint_greedy.

Intuition (proposed method): greedily pack pairwise-disjoint child balls inside each parent node so that every accepted child captures many local points while staying well within the parent’s radius budget. The builder repeatedly seeds a candidate centre, expands its ball until either the radius_divisor cap or a sibling boundary is met, then locks the child and moves on to the next best candidate. Because every parent may accept more than two children, the resulting tree is naturally \(k\)-ary when the data supports it.

Helper interplay:

  • Builds a mandatory local KDTree to accelerate radius queries while honouring the greedy radius_divisor cap; the module raises a runtime error when scikit-learn is unavailable, keeping the routine squarely in the KD-tree regime.

  • Uses utils.meb.meb() for minimum enclosing balls at leaves and whenever a candidate cluster needs re-enclosing.

  • Relies on utils.geometry.enclose_many_balls() to tighten parent balls once children are locked in.

Complexity: constructing the KD-tree costs \(O(m \log m)\) per internal node with \(m\) local points, and each greedy radius query is \(O(\log m + s)\) where s is the number of neighbours returned. The number of admitted children k is typically small, so the KD-tree acceleration keeps the routine tractable on medium-sized datasets.

Package entry-points¶

Module: gal.trees.

Intuition: expose a uniform registry so callers can request any builder with gal.trees.build_tree or use the convenience build_ball_tree shortcut for the disjoint-greedy strategy. The package also publishes AVAILABLE_METHODS for discoverability.

Helper interplay:

  • build_tree looks up the chosen method inside AVAILABLE_METHODS and forwards keyword arguments unchanged to the underlying module.

  • build_ball_tree normalises legacy keyword arguments (k, P, and radius_divisor) into a configuration dictionary before delegating to gal.trees.disjoint_greedy.

Complexity: the registry lookup runs in constant time before handing control to whichever builder is selected.

Legacy compatibility: the historical gal.trees.ball_tree module remains as a thin shim that re-exports build_tree and build_ball_tree from gal.trees, so existing imports continue to work unchanged.

Search primitives¶

Module: gal.search.

Intuition: ship a modular branch-and-bound engine whose queue objective and bounding strategy can be injected. The default configuration reproduces the behaviour described in the paper while allowing experiments with alternative pruning heuristics.

Helper interplay:

  • gal.search.engine.Search accepts optional bounder and objective instances, defaulting to gal.search.bounds.AngularBounds and gal.search.objectives.LowerBoundObjective.

  • The engine gathers leaf statistics and, when requested, falls back to an exhaustive check within the tau threshold to guarantee optimality.

Complexity: identical to the legacy implementation - dual-tree traversal with sub-linear pruning when bounds remain tight.

Testing strategy¶

The test-suite in tests/ documents the behavioural contract and is designed to be read alongside the builders:

  • tests/test_enclosure.py performs depth-first traversals for random, duplicated, and collinear datasets under both MEB backends. It asserts that every node radius covers all of its descendant points within a \(10^{-9}\) tolerance.

  • tests/test_builders_api.py checks the user-facing API: each builder must return a populated GeometricTree, propagate default or overridden leaf sizes, and record the selected MEB backend.

  • tests/test_builders_correctness.py verifies structural invariants and the PCA balance heuristic. It ensures that leaves respect leaf_size, that no recursion emits empty children, and that the Ball* configuration chooses a split with a strictly smaller sum of child radii on an elongated synthetic dataset.

References¶

[Omohundro1989] (1,2,3)

Omohundro, S. M. Five Balltree Construction Algorithms. ICSI Technical Report TR-89-063, 1989.

[Moore2000] (1,2)

Moore, A. W. The Anchors Hierarchy: Using the Triangle Inequality to Survive High Dimensional Data. CMU-RI-TR-00-05, 2000.

[Dolatshah2015]

Dolatshah, M., Hadian, A., and Minaei-Bidgoli, B. Ball-tree: Efficient spatial indexing for constrained nearest-neighbor search in metric spaces. arXiv:1511.00628, 2015.

[Welzl1991]

Welzl, E. Smallest Enclosing Disks (Balls and Ellipsoids) in H. Maurer (ed.), New Results and New Trends in Computer Science, 1991.
